summary: Seven small islands seventy miles west of Key West, reached only by boat or seaplane. Massive, unfinished Fort Jefferson fills one of them; around them lie clear water, seagrass and the least disturbed coral reefs in the Florida Keys.

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip, or a night camping on Garden Key

story: The Dry Tortugas are the westernmost and most isolated of the Florida Keys: low islands of coral sand at the edge of the Gulf of Mexico, almost all of the park's hundred square miles open water. Juan Ponce de León named them in 1513 for the sea turtles his crew caught, and sailors added Dry for the lack of fresh water.

On Garden Key stands Fort Jefferson, begun in the 1840s to guard the shipping lane through the Florida Straits and never finished. It is the largest brick masonry structure in the Western Hemisphere, built of more than sixteen million bricks. During and after the Civil War it held prisoners, among them Dr. Samuel Mudd, convicted for his part in the Lincoln assassination conspiracy.

The reefs here have shipwrecked vessels for centuries and are among the healthiest in Florida. Sea turtles nest on the beaches, and every spring and summer tens of thousands of sooty terns and brown noddies nest on Bush Key; migrating songbirds stop over on their way across the Gulf. John James Audubon came to see the birds in 1832.

The fort became a national monument in 1935, and the monument a national park in 1992. Part of the park is a research natural area where nothing may be taken, so the reefs can be studied as they would be without fishing.

sights.name: Fort Jefferson
sights.note: A six-sided brick fortress with a moat, filling most of Garden Key; walk the casemates and the top of the walls.

sights.name: Dr. Mudd's Cell
sights.note: Where Samuel Mudd was held after the Lincoln assassination trial.

sights.name: Garden Key
sights.note: Beaches and snorkelling along the fort's moat wall, where coral and fish gather.

sights.name: Loggerhead Key
sights.note: The largest island, with a tall lighthouse and a reef offshore, reached by private boat or kayak.

sights.name: Windjammer Wreck
sights.note: The remains of an iron-hulled sailing ship on Loggerhead Reef, a dive site.

sights.name: Little Africa Patch Reef
sights.note: A patch reef off Loggerhead Key, good snorkelling in calm conditions.

entrances: By the park's concession ferry from Key West, by seaplane, or by private or chartered boat
planYourVisit.reservations: Ferry and seaplane seats and the small Garden Key campground fill early. Book well ahead.
lodging: No lodging; camping on Garden Key only, with everything brought in, including water
seasonalClosures: Bush Key closes to visitors while the terns nest; winter fronts bring rough seas, and June to November is hurricane season

chronology.text: Juan Ponce de León names the islands for their sea turtles.
Work begins on a lighthouse on Garden Key.
John James Audubon visits to study the nesting birds.
Fort Jefferson National Monument is proclaimed.
The monument becomes Dry Tortugas National Park.

safety: There is no fresh water, food or shelter for sale. Bring water, sun protection and everything else you need.
Currents can be strong off the islands. Snorkel with a partner and stay near the beach and moat wall.
regulations: Coral, shells and artifacts may not be taken; in the Research Natural Area nothing may be taken at all.
Drones may not be launched, landed or flown in the park.
